questions.questionText: Does it concern vectors?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Actually, it directly deals with vectors.

questions.questionText: Is it a ‘specific’ vector (e.g., the zero vector) or a set of vectors?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Well, it’s an expression involving vectors, but not a single one or a set.

questions.questionText: Is it an operation/expression?
questions.correctiveFeedback: It is indeed an expression formed with vectors and scalars.

questions.questionText: Does it preserve scalar multiplication and vector addition?
questions.correctiveFeedback: That is actually the ‘linearity property’, and linear combinations always preserve it.

questions.questionText: Does it always work with two vectors?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Actually, you can combine any number of vectors, not just two.

questions.questionText: Does it produce a set of vectors?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Careful, it produces exactly one vector after the combination.

questions.questionText: Does it involve coefficients/scalars?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Scalars are essential to forming a linear combination.

questions.questionText: Are the coefficients always positive numbers?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Coefficients can be negative or zero too.

questions.questionText: Are the coefficients always integers?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Coefficients can be any real numbers.

questions.questionText: So, all real numbers?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Coefficients can be any real numbers.

questions.questionText: Even zero?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Even zero scalars are allowed in a linear combination.

questions.questionText: When drawing, can we use the parallelogram law?
questions.correctiveFeedback: The parallelogram law is exactly how vector addition works in linear combinations.

terms.finalMessage: Looks like I figured it out! It's a linear combination of vectors!

questions.questionText: Does it concern vectors?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Actually, the span is a set of vectors.

questions.questionText: Is it a vector operation?
questions.correctiveFeedback: The span is a set, not an operation.

questions.questionText: Is it a ‘specific’ vector (e.g., the zero vector)?
questions.correctiveFeedback: The span is not a single vector.

questions.questionText: Is it a set of vectors?
questions.correctiveFeedback: The span is always a set of vectors.

questions.questionText: Is this ‘magic set’ somehow ‘generated’ by a set of vectors S?
questions.correctiveFeedback: The span is exactly the set generated by S.

questions.questionText: Does the set S always contain two or three vectors?
questions.correctiveFeedback: S can have any number of vectors, even just one.

questions.questionText: Can the set S contain just one vector?
questions.correctiveFeedback: One vector generates a line through the origin.

questions.questionText: If S contains 3 vectors, does this ‘magic set’ always equal to ℝ³?
questions.correctiveFeedback: 3 vectors may not span all of ℝ³ if they’re dependent.

questions.questionText: But I need at least 3 vectors to generate ℝ³?
questions.correctiveFeedback: You do need at least 3 vectors, with only two, you wouldn't generate more than a plane.

questions.questionText: And if these 3 vectors are linearly independent, then the ‘magic set’ equals ℝ³?
questions.correctiveFeedback: 3 independent vectors do span all of ℝ³.

questions.questionText: Is this ‘magic set’ a set of all finite linear combinations of the given vectors?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Wrong—that’s exactly what the span is.

terms.finalMessage: Then it must be the span!

questions.questionText: Does it concern vectors?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Actually, it’s a set of vectors.

questions.questionText: Is it a vector operation?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Think again. A basis is not an operation but a set of vectors.

questions.questionText: Is it a ‘specific’ vector (e.g., the zero vector)?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Actually, it’s not just one vector…

questions.questionText: Is it a set of vectors?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Actually, a basis is a set of vectors.

questions.questionText: Does the ‘magic set’ generate (span) the whole ℝⁿ, where n is the dimension of the vectors?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Remember, a basis must generate the whole space it belongs to.

questions.questionText: To generate ℝ³, would the ‘magic set’ always be {(1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0), (0, 0, 1)}?
questions.correctiveFeedback:
Actually, there are infinitely many options, 
e.g., {(2, 1, 5), (1, -1, 3), (0, 2, -1)} also works.

questions.questionText: Can the set contain more vectors than the dimension of the space?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Actually, a basis has exactly as many vectors as the dimension.

questions.questionText: Can one of the vectors in the set be written as a combination of the others?
questions.correctiveFeedback: The basis is the minimal set that generates the space. If one can be written as a combination of the others, then it's redundant.

questions.questionText: Ah, so the set is linearly independent?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Linear independence is a key property for a basis.

questions.questionText: Can we use them to describe the coordinates of any vector in the space?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Actually, yes, the basis vectors form a coordinate system for the space.

terms.finalMessage: Looks like I figured it out! It's the basis of a vector space!
